files.lesson.md: --- order: 4 unit: angle-sums node: AC9M7M05 n1 title: Angles in a triangle summary: However you change a triangle, its three angles add to 180°. Tear off the corners and they make a straight line. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A roof truss, a bike frame, a folded paper plane: triangles of every shape. Squash one and its angles change. Does anything about them stay the same?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8162 url: http://127.0.0.1:8162/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: geo.yml#explain-pic, caption: "An obtuse triangle: $24° + 127° + 29° = 180°$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@geo.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "A triangle's angles add to 180°" say: "A triangle's three angles always add to one hundred and eighty degrees." clip: - caption: { text: "This triangle: the three angles add to 180°.", say: "In this triangle, the three angles add to one hundred and eighty." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Make one angle big. The others shrink: still 180°.", say: "Make one angle big, and the others shrink. Still one eighty." } - click: Obtuse - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Very flat: still 180°.", say: "Even a very flat triangle: still one eighty." } - click: Very flat - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Why? Tear off the corners: they make a straight line.", say: "Why? Tear off the corners, and they make a straight line." } - click: Tear off the corners - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "= 180°" } - wait: 1500 --- An **angle** measures a turn, in degrees ($°$). A full turn is $360°$, and the angles on a straight line add to $180°$. A triangle has three corners, so three angles inside it. Change the triangle's shape and the angles change, but what happens to their total? ## Predict: a stretched triangle ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what happens to the total before dragging makes the board a test of their idea, not a demonstration." check: type: predict q: "You drag one corner of a triangle so one angle gets much bigger. What happens to the total of the three angles?" options: - "It stays the same" - "It gets bigger" - "It gets smaller" - "It depends on how long the sides are" actual: "It stays the same: 180°. As one angle grows, the other two shrink by exactly as much." ``` Picture a triangle you could pull out into a long, thin shape. Which angles change? ## Run: change the triangle ```step stage: run insight: "Dragging the corners and watching the total shows that the angles change but their sum never does." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag the corners until one angle is more than $120°$. What is the total now?", when: "m > 120" } ``` Drag any corner to a new dot. The board measures each angle and adds them up under the triangle. Make tall, wide and flat triangles. Was your prediction right? ## Investigate: why 180°? ```step stage: investigate try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#tear", height: 720 } insight: "Tearing off the corners and putting them side by side shows why the total is fixed: the three angles fill a straight line, which is 180°. Kai's mistake ties the angles to the side lengths." tasks: - starter: "geo.yml#tear" check: { type: board, text: "Press **Tear off the corners**. Then drag a corner and watch the torn pieces.", when: "t = 1" } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kai" text: "Kai compares a small triangle with one twice as big. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: angle-sum-size explain: "Line 3: making every side twice as long does not change the angles, only the size. The big triangle's angles are still 50°, 60° and 70°, adding to 180°." - check: type: question q: "Why do the three torn corners always make a straight line?" options: ["Because the angles add to $180°$, and a straight line is $180°$", "Because every triangle has a $90°$ angle", "Because the corners are all the same size"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Try the board: many triangles have no right angle.", "Look at the torn pieces: they are often different sizes."] explain: "Side by side at one point, the three angles fill a straight line exactly. Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so the triangle's angles do too." ``` ### Tear off the corners Here is the argument, the way you would do it with a paper triangle. ```worked \text{Draw any triangle} :: Cut it out of paper, and mark its three angles A, B and C. \text{Tear off the three corners} :: Each piece keeps one angle. \text{Put the points together} :: Place the three corners side by side, all touching at one point. \text{They fill a straight line} :: The outside edges of A and C line up into one straight line. A + B + C = 180° :: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so the triangle's angles do too. ``` On the board, press **Tear off the corners**, then drag a corner. The pieces change, but they always fill the line. ### Find the mistake Read Kai's working one line at a time. Which line ties the angles to the length of the sides? ### Why a straight line? ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a right angle (the other two must make 90°), a very flat triangle (the other two are tiny), then two edge cases that the 180° rule decides." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#right", height: 720 } tasks: - starter: "geo.yml#right" hint: ["A right angle is a square corner. Use the dots: one side across, one side straight up.", "Put C straight above A."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a triangle with a right angle ($90°$). What do the other two angles add to?", when: "m = 90", explain: "The other two add to 90°: 180° − 90°." } - starter: "geo.yml#flat" hint: "Pull one corner until the triangle is nearly a line. Tear off the corners to see the pieces." check: { type: board, text: "Make a triangle with an angle of more than $150°$. How big are the other two?", when: "m > 150", explain: "Less than 30° together: the big angle leaves very little of the 180°." } - check: type: answer q: "A triangle has three equal angles. How big is each one?" answer: "60" feedback: - ["90", "Three angles of 90° would add to 270°."] - ["180", "180° is the total. Share it between three equal angles."] explain: "180° ÷ 3 = 60°." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "What do the three angles of any triangle add to, in degrees?", answer: 180, tolerance: 0, explain: "180°. Three equal angles share that between them." } - check: type: question q: "Edge case: can a triangle have two right angles?" options: ["No: two right angles already make $180°$, leaving $0°$ for the third", "Yes, if it is big enough", "Yes, if the third angle is very small"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Size does not change the angles. Add the two right angles: what is left for the third?", "The third angle would have to be 0°. Try it on the board: the sides would never meet."] explain: "90° + 90° = 180°, so the third angle would be 0°: the two sides would be parallel and never meet." ``` ### A right angle Each task changes one thing. First: make a square corner. ### Very flat Now make one angle very big. ### Three equal angles ### Two right angles? ## Practise: use the rule ```step stage: practise insight: "Recognising possible triangles, a measurement that is nearly 180°, and the size question, mixed; the review keeps angles on a straight line from Year 6 fresh." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which three angles could be the angles of a triangle?" options: ["$40°, 60°, 80°$", "$50°, 60°, 80°$", "$90°, 90°, 10°$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Add them: 190°. A triangle's angles add to 180°.", "Add them: 190°, and two right angles leave nothing for the third."] explain: "40° + 60° + 80° = 180°." - check: type: question q: "Lia measures a paper triangle with a protractor: $57°, 68°, 56°$. That adds to $181°$. What is the best explanation?" options: ["Her measurements are a little out: a protractor reads to about a degree", "Her triangle is a special one that adds to $181°$", "She has measured the wrong angles"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Every triangle's angles add to exactly 180°. What about the measuring?", "Possibly, but 181° is so close to 180° that small measuring errors are the likely reason."] explain: "Real measurements are rounded. 181° is within a degree or two of 180°, which is what measuring three angles by hand gives." - check: type: question q: "Triangle P has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. Triangle Q has sides 30 cm, 40 cm and 50 cm. How do their angle sums compare?" options: ["They are the same: $180°$", "Q's is 10 times bigger", "Q's is bigger, but not 10 times"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Longer sides do not make the angles bigger: Q is P enlarged, with the same angles.", "The angles of Q are the same as P's; only the sides are longer."] explain: "Every triangle's angles add to 180°. Q is P made 10 times bigger, with exactly the same angles." - check: type: answer q: "Review: two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is $130°$. How big is the other?" answer: "50" feedback: - ["230", "Angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 360°."] - ["130", "Together they make a straight line, 180°. How much is left after 130°?"] explain: "180° − 130° = 50°." ``` ### Possible? ### Measuring by hand ### Bigger triangle ### Review ## Make: one angle equals the other two ```step stage: make insight: "Building a triangle where one angle equals the other two together reverses the lesson: from the 180° rule to a shape it forces, a right angle." try: { playground: board, starter: "geo.yml#make", height: 600 } hint: ["If one angle equals the other two added together, it is half of the total.", "Half of 180° is 90°: make a square corner."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a triangle where one angle is exactly the other two added together.", when: "m = 90", explain: "If one angle equals the other two together, it is half of 180°: a right angle. Here 90° = the other two added." } ``` Think first: if one angle is the other two added together, what fraction of $180°$ is it? Then build it. Stretch: can a triangle have one angle that is exactly twice the sum of the other two? How big is it? ## Make: a garden bed, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A triangle's angles add to 180° and angles on a straight line add to 180°, so a path along a straight side needs both reasons." hint: ["Find the third angle of the bed first.", "The path makes a straight line with one side of the bed."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A triangular garden bed has two corners of 52° and 67°. A path runs straight along the bed's bottom side and past the corner C, so it makes a straight line with that side. What is the angle between the path and the bed's other side at C, in degrees?" steps: - ["The angles of the bed add to 180°, so the angle at C is 180 − 52 − 67 = 61°", "angles in a triangle add to 180°"] - ["The path and the bed's side make a straight line, so the angle outside is 180 − 61 = 119°", "angles on a straight line add to 180°"] picks: - step: 1 q: "Why is the angle at C 61°?" options: - "Angles in a triangle add to 180°, so it is what is left after 52° and 67°" - "Angles on a straight line add to 180°" - "The three angles of the bed are equal" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A straight line is used in the second step. The bed's own three corners add to 180° too.", "The three corners are 52°, 67° and C, which are not equal."] answer: "119" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["61", "That is the angle inside the bed at C. The path makes a straight line with the side, so take 61° from 180°."] - ["128", "That is 180 − 52. Find the angle at C first: 180 − 52 − 67, then use the straight line."] criteria: - "I found the third angle of the bed first and gave the reason." - "I gave a second reason for the path: a straight line." - "I checked that 119° is also 52° + 67°." explain: "C = 180 − 52 − 67 = 61°. The angle outside is on a straight line with it: 180 − 61 = 119°. It also equals the other two angles, 52 + 67." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The bed and the angles are made up for the task. Sketch it, write each step with its reason, then type the angle. ```teacher summary: Students drag triangles of every shape on a dot grid, see that the three angles always add to 180°, and explain why by tearing off the corners to make a straight line (AC9M7M05, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can show that the angles of a triangle add to 180°, by measuring and by tearing off the corners. - I can explain why this is true for every triangle, whatever its shape or size. - I can tell whether three angles could be the angles of a triangle. struggle: Trusting 180 when a triangle looks very different. Ask students to tear off the three corners and line them up on a straight line. before: > Do the Run board and the tear-off task yourself first. Students should know that angles on a straight line add to 180° (Year 6). The board measures to the nearest degree and shares out the rounding so the shown angles add to the shown total. With a real protractor, totals of 178° to 182° are normal: say so when students measure by hand (Practise has a question on it). If you have time, do the paper version too: every student draws a different triangle, tears off the corners and lines them up. Seeing 25 different triangles all make a straight line is the strongest evidence. The formal proof with parallel lines comes with AC9M7M04. Finding a missing angle from the other two is the next step in class (node 3), not this lesson. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 'it gets bigger' are thinking of the big angle only. Do not correct it yet." - "Run: ask students to make the tallest, the widest and the flattest triangle they can, and to read the total each time." - "Investigate: model the worked example live with a paper triangle: mark the three angles, tear them off at writing pace, and put the points together on a ruler's edge, saying each step. Then show the board's torn pieces changing as a corner moves." - "Modify: before the right-angle task ask: if one angle is 90°, what must the other two add to? Then check on the board." - "Practise: Lia's measurement question is a chance to talk about measuring error, which science lessons need too." - "Make: ask a student to explain why the angle must be 90° before anyone builds it." - "Make on paper: ask for the reason at each step, then ask why 119 is also 52 plus 67." stuck: - see: A student thinks a bigger triangle has bigger angles (Kai's mistake). ask: If you make a photocopy twice as big, do the corners get pointier or blunter? fix: "Enlarge a triangle on the board by doubling each corner's coordinates: the angles stay the same." - see: A student adds the angles and gets 179° or 181° with a protractor. ask: How accurately can you read a protractor? fix: Each reading can be a degree out, so three readings can be two or three degrees out. The true total is 180°. - see: A student says the rule only works for the triangles they tried. ask: Which triangle could you try that would break it? fix: "Let them try their 'breaking' triangle on the board or on paper. Then point to the torn corners: they always fill a straight line, whatever the shape." stretch: "Can a triangle have one angle that is twice the other two added together? (Yes: 120°, since 120 = 2 × 60.) What about three times? (135°.)" support: Use the Run board throughout, and the preset buttons are on the explain clip's board. Give students paper triangles to tear. leads: > Next: angles in any polygon, by splitting it into triangles. Where it leads: finding unknown angles with reasons (node 3), the proof with parallel lines (AC9M7M04), and why regular hexagons tessellate. exit: q: A student says the angles of a very large triangle add to more than 180°. Explain why they are wrong. a: "Every triangle's angles add to 180°: tear off the corners and they fill a straight line. Size changes the sides, not the angles." explain: > The three angles of **any** triangle add to $180°$. When you change a triangle's shape, one angle grows and the others shrink by exactly as much. Making it bigger without changing its shape does not change the angles at all. Why? Tear off the three corners and put their points together: they fill a straight line, and angles on a straight line add to $180°$. ```

# region: kai
Kai draws a small triangle, then one with every side twice as long.
Small triangle: 50° + 60° + 70° = 180°.
The big triangle has longer sides, so its angles are bigger.
So the big triangle's angles add to more than 180°.
